title: Beyond the 956: Army to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead azide in Iowa today
excerpt: The U.S. Army will conduct a controlled, in-place detonation of 68 drums of degraded, crystallized lead azide — more than 9,700 pounds of net explosive weight — at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, today, Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at approximately 9:00 a.m. CST.
content:
🌎 BEYOND THE 956

The U.S. Army is set to carry out a controlled, in-place detonation of 68 drums of degraded, crystallized lead azide — more than 9,700 pounds of net explosive weight — at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, today, Wednesday, November 25, 2026, at approximately 9:00 a.m. CST.

Lead azide is a primary explosive used in munitions. The material was found during a routine safety inspection in March 2026, when inspectors discovered severe degradation and crystallization in the stored drums. In that crystallized state, the explosive has become so unstable that it cannot be moved, treated, or transported safely, according to the Army. A chemical-neutralization contract with MuniRem Environmental was cancelled over safety concerns.

The Army says a controlled detonation is the only viable option. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said every expert agency agrees that a planned, mitigated detonation is far preferable to a spontaneous, uncontrolled explosion of the material. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds concurs with that assessment.

The detonation has been delayed twice. It was originally scheduled for November 20, then moved to November 23, and is now set for today, the day before Thanksgiving.

The plan has drawn a legal fight. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals paused the Environmental Protection Agency's emergency permit after environmental groups — the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa, represented by Earthjustice — sued. The Army is proceeding under an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion. Gov.-elect Rob Sand has also been involved in the dispute, and President Donald Trump has weighed in.

Out of an abundance of caution, the Federal Emergency Management Agency is supporting a recommended relocation for residents of Middletown, a town of about 400 people, and surrounding areas within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant. The relocation began November 24. FEMA is providing funded hotel accommodations through Friday, November 27, along with food, water, and emergency transportation. Affected residents can register at DisasterAssistance.gov or by calling 1-800-621-3362.

Officials warn that a lead-dust plume from the blast is predicted to travel up to 100 miles, toward southeastern Iowa and northern Missouri, possibly reaching the Mississippi River. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services advises residents in the area to stay indoors with windows and doors closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation and to wet-clean surfaces afterward.

The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is a World War II-era facility on about 19,000 acres in Des Moines County in southeastern Iowa.

Update — November 25, 2026

The detonation went ahead as planned on Wednesday morning. The U.S. Army said it detonated the 68 barrels of degraded lead azide — nearly 10,000 pounds — at about 9 a.m. at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, and called the operation a success. Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said at an 11 a.m. news conference that all of the lead azide was destroyed, with no secondary explosions, no kickout of material, and no damage to infrastructure in or around the plant.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency reported no detection of airborne lead in the area. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said initial readings were 0.0, and Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds said in a statement that the EPA had confirmed zero detection of airborne lead in the region. The Des Moines Register reported that Middletown was quiet more than 90 minutes after the blast, with no known reports of broken residential windows or structural damage, no visible dust, and no lingering odor. Residents who sheltered in place or at the Armed Forces Reserve Center felt two consecutive booms around 9 a.m.

Monitoring will continue until the environment is confirmed safe, and workers will begin collecting samples, Zeldin said. The Army said the threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated.

Update — November 26, 2026

Residents were given the all-clear on Wednesday evening. The U.S. Army announced the all-clear just after 6:30 p.m. Eastern time, saying government mapping had detected zero airborne lead, and a joint release from FEMA said the shelter-in-place order had been lifted and residents in the affected area could safely resume normal activities. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said its monitoring showed no airborne lead in the hours after the detonation, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the department would continue working with Iowa officials and federal partners to assess potential health risks and share findings. Post-detonation surface sampling was underway, with results to be released once complete, the Army said. FEMA had offered lodging to residents who chose to leave through Friday, November 27.

Update — Thursday, November 26, 2026

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday that its air monitors continued to report zero detection of airborne lead across the region, and that its teams had collected 1,591 air, water, soil and dust samples before the detonation and more than 1,000 samples since about 1 p.m. Central time on Wednesday. More than 130 structures sampled before the blast were sampled again after it, the agency said, and crews were sampling schools, playgrounds, daycares and churches on Thursday, with a second round of drinking-water sampling underway. The EPA said it expects to start receiving lab results on the post-detonation samples as early as Friday, November 27.

Sources: U.S. Army; CNN; Des Moines Register; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; Office of Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds; The Associated Press; FEMA; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
